ruler_count: A single crown, and no one alive who can seriously argue with it.
A crowned ruler and a handful of under-kings who obey when it suits them.
Two claimants sharing one throne, each with a separate household and seal.
A small council of near-equals who must all agree before anything moves.
A great assembly where every landholder with a spear and a grudge may speak.
One monarch, one regent, and a child whose name decides everything.
A council of elders drawn from the great households, ruling by rough consensus.
A warlord and the captains who could replace him by morning.
A hall of clan chiefs, each master of his own valley and none of the others.
Three rival hierarchs who rule jointly and plot without pause.
A single priest-king, attended by an assembly that may only advise.
A confederation of free towns, each sending a delegate to a standing assembly.
ruler_class: Old landed families who trace their claim through a dozen marriages.
Merchant houses whose ledgers hold more leverage than any banner.
Sorcerers who trade in secrets and never explain their methods.
A bloodline in which the gift appears in every second generation.
Guild artisans who took the city in a single bloody week.
A hill people long accustomed to ruling the lowlands they conquered.
Priests of a temple that owns a third of the farmland.
Citizens of the old capital, who alone hold a vote in the assembly.
Mounted herders from the eastern plains, still despised by the farmers.
War captains who never went home after the last war.
Clan heads of a dozen feuding kindreds.
The factor of a distant power, seated in a borrowed palace.
Freeholders who bought their charters and their privileges outright.
A knightly order that swore to protect the realm and stayed to run it.
Riverboat magnates who control the grain barges.
Magesmiths whose forges arm every army on the border.
A league of sea captains who own more hulls than the crown.
Foreign-born officers of a legion that no longer has a homeland.
Shrine-keepers of a roadside god who became a war cult.
Creditors who hold titles as security against unpaid loans.
Widows and dowagers of the great houses, ruling through sons and stewards.
A guild of record-keepers who alone know who owns what.
ruler_legitimacy: They have held the seat so long that no one remembers the alternative.
They are believed wiser than their rivals, and the belief is untested.
They won every battle they were ever asked to fight.
The temple anointed them before a crowd that filled the whole square.
The great households chose them, and the choosing was witnessed.
They ended a famine, and the story has grown in the telling.
They broke the last rebellion and displayed the heads for a season.
They reopened the roads and the markets and the mines.
They pulled down the old order, and no one wants it back.
They made the highways safe, and travelers still call it a miracle.
They won a war of conquest that filled the treasury.
No one can name a better candidate, and everyone has tried.
A prophecy names them, and the prophecy is inconveniently specific.
They hold the only tax rolls and the only key to the granary.
They married into every great house that might have opposed them.
They were chosen by lot, and the lot is assumed to be divine.
They are the last heir of a line that ruled for three centuries.
They are feared, and fear has passed for right across six generations.
They keep the border clans paid, and the border clans keep them.
They were elected for one year and simply never left.
An old treaty names their house as arbiter in all disputes.
ruler_control: Lesser lords who hold their land on condition of answering a summons.
Clerks and reeves drawn from commoner families and loyal to the office.
Enforcers whose authority comes from a charm they cannot remove.
A temple hierarchy that preaches obedience in every village.
Judges whose rulings are obeyed even by the great houses.
A pack of sworn brutes kept hungry and pointed at trouble.
Granary wardens and toll-keepers who decide who eats and who trades.
Priests who pronounce blessings and withhold them.
Habit, mostly; people obey before they think to ask why.
Hired blades, retained by the season and paid in plunder.
Court sorcerers who read the letters and remember all of them.
A client people settled among the natives and armed for the purpose.
Hostages taken from every great household and raised in the capital.
Village headmen who owe their posts to the crown and know it.
Marriage alliances that make rebellion a family quarrel.
The right to name heirs, which every house needs and none can buy.
A mounted patrol that rides the same roads on the same days.
Oaths sworn on relics, which the oath-breakers genuinely believe in.
Control of the salt pans and the good iron.
Wardens of the mountain passes, who can close a road with a word.
single_ruler_form: A crowned monarch who rules through lesser lords sworn to the throne.
An autocrat who staffs the offices with commoners and keeps the nobles at court.
A war-leader elected for a season, and re-elected for eleven seasons running.
A warlord whose only claim is that no one has beaten him yet.
The eldest surviving head of the ruling house, chosen by the kindred.
A high priest who speaks for a god and is never contradicted aloud.
A monarch bound to a fixed term, whose term keeps being extended.
A wielder of a relic crown that no other head can wear.
A steward ruling in the name of a king nobody has seen in years.
A judge-king who hears petitions in the square each morning.
A queen dowager acting as regent for a son who will never be old enough.
A hunt-master of the clans, chosen for skill and obeyed for luck.
A tribute-collector of a distant hegemon, styled as a king at home.
A blind oracle kept in a palace and interpreted by three scribes.
A lord admiral of a river fleet that no inland power can match.
A master of the mint whose face is on every coin in circulation.
multiple_ruler_form: Peers of the realm, meeting by ancient right and voting by household.
The senior heads of the ruling class, who decide by seniority and grudge.
An elected bench of magnates, chosen for life by the great households.
Hereditary heirs to seats that have not changed hands in centuries.
War captains whose votes are counted in companies, not in heads.
Oligarchs of the great merchant houses, deciding by bloc and bribe.
Temple delegates who must agree unanimously or the city stops.
Ministers chosen by the ruler and confirmed by a show of hands.
A council of clan mothers who sit until they agree.
Two houses sharing one seat, alternating by year and hating every moment.
A conclave of guildmasters, one vote per trade, all of them bought.
A war council of the ruler's marshals, which has begun to outlive its war.
An assembly of freeholders who must be summoned and fed before they vote.
A synod of elders who rule by interpretation of an old text.
A regency council of five, of whom two are already dead and unmentioned.
government_struggle: The ruler is whittling down a lord whose retainers outnumber the crown's.
The chief minister has been quietly appointing his own kin to every office.
A grand campaign of conquest has stalled at a siege that will not end.
An envoy insulted a neighboring court, and the insult has been remembered.
A usurper holds the loyalty of the capital guard and has not yet said so.
A rival power is paying the border lords to make noise.
The merchant houses demand seats, and they have the money to be heard.
The old families want the powers they lost two reigns ago.
A caste of laborers is being worked to ruin and has begun to organize.
A food shortage has turned grumbling into talk of replacing the ruler.
The last ruler's failed war is still being paid for, and the bills are due.
The heir is a fool, and half the court has already chosen an alternative.
The temple wants the right to name the next ruler.
Two provinces are feuding over a border the crown drew badly.
The army has not been paid since the last harvest.
A popular preacher condemns the court from a roadside pulpit.
The royal household itself is split between the ruler's two consorts.
A guild has bought the tax farmers, and the revenue has thinned to nothing.
The old capital resents the new one and says so in every tavern.
A general has begun to answer orders with questions.
government_recent_event: A treasurer was hanged for treason, and the accounts he kept have vanished.
An heir was born after eleven years of hoping, and every faction is recalculating.
The chief minister fell from favor in a single afternoon, and no one will say why.
A great lord refused a summons and rode home with all his retainers.
The temple was publicly slighted at a feast, and the priests have not forgotten.
An allied court was insulted by a badly worded letter and recalled its envoy.
A ring of foreign agents was uncovered inside the household guard.
A great fortress was announced, and the levy to pay for it is already being taken.
The officials trusted with a new road spent the money on their own estates.
A new office of inspectors was created and given power over every market.
A levy was laid on hearths and hearth-tools, and the villages are furious.
A general was dismissed for a defeat he did not cause and will not forget.
A bandit chief has become a hero in the songs, and the songs are spreading.
A bridge and a wall were begun with great ceremony and no clear plan.
A wealthy fief was granted to a favorite, and the neighbors are counting spears.
Three merchant houses were fined into ruin over a smuggling charge no one believes.
Assassins struck at a provincial governor and left a note claiming a higher authority.
The faction that ran the treasury has collapsed, and its rivals are dividing the offices.
A whole house of scribes was dismissed, and its clerks are now for hire.
The province borders were redrawn overnight, and two lords now claim the same mill.
The crown seized a monastery's lands to pay its soldiers, and the monks preach against it.
A royal progress was cut short by a rockslide that looked carefully arranged.
The ruler's guard was doubled, and the reason given changes by the day.
A daughter was married to a border lord to buy his silence, and his rivals are insulted.
A census was ordered, and the villages are hiding people, grain, and cattle.
The mint debased the coin, and prices in the market have doubled in a month.
A famous relic was carried to the capital, and the town it left is threatening revolt.
An assembly was dissolved before it could vote and has not been called again.
A ship's captain was raised to command the fleet over every real sailor's objection.
The crown forgave a rebellion wholesale, and the loyalists who suffered are furious.
A great granary was opened to feed the army, and the winter has not yet begun.
A judge was removed for ruling against the crown, and the courts have gone quiet.
A truce was signed with an old enemy, and the soldiers are being sent home unpaid.
government_officials_problem: Tax farmers who take the levy twice and the receipt once.
Garrison troops who have begun charging tolls on their own roads.
Magistrates who sell rulings to whichever party pays last.
Informers who report on neighbors and settle old scores.
Tithe collectors who count the harvest before the farmer does.
Market wardens who set the weights and own the scales.
Noble retinues that ride through the market and take what they please.
Constables who have started arresting people for their purses.
Inquisitors who see sorcery in every hearth and every herb garden.
Road wardens who have begun behaving as though the road is theirs.
Court scholars who teach that the old laws no longer bind anyone.
Village headmen who have made themselves small kings.
Harbor masters who charge by the crate and by the crate's contents.
Provisioners who sell the army's grain and report it stolen.
Tax assessors who value land by the owner's manners.
Border captains who collect from both sides of the line.
Clerks who lose the records of their enemies and find them later.
Grain inspectors who condemn good wheat and then buy it cheap.
Hereditary gate-keepers who charge entry to a free city.
Census takers who count households twice and coin once.
government_minister_problem: The chief minister runs a private network of clients against his rivals.
The council meets monthly, decides nothing, and signs whatever is set before it.
Half the ministers were executed last spring and the rest have learned silence.
Two ministers are taking payment from a court that has just declared war.
The council is split three ways and cannot agree on so much as a clerk.
The ruler has stopped attending and the ministers now rule in his name.
The ministers have quietly taken over appointments and none of them mention it.
The whole bench is committed to a war the treasury cannot pay for.
One minister has proof of another's treason and is saving it for the right moment.
The youngest minister is the ruler's nephew and outranks every capable man.
The ministers are competent and hate one another more than they fear the ruler.
The council's own guards now take orders from a captain no one appointed.
Two of the ministers are one man's clients and always vote as one.
The ministers have begun issuing orders the ruler has never seen.
A purge was promised and never carried out, so everyone is waiting.
ruler_established: Newly seated, and already asking who can be trusted.
An outsider who came to power with no allies but the men who carried him.
Ascended this season, and the great houses are still taking his measure.
Held in place by one marriage, two promises, and a great deal of luck.
Backed by a hard core of retainers who have nowhere else to go.
Secure among the soldiers, unknown among the priests.
Supported by a network of clients in every province and every guild.
So long in power that courtiers have forgotten how to flatter anyone else.
Ten years on the seat, and the last plot against it is a decade old.
The only ruler most of the people have ever seen.
Recognized by treaty abroad, which props up the claim at home.
Ruling through a regency and holding the regency by force of will.
Third of their line to hold the seat, and the first obeyed without argument.
government_stability: Collapsing: orders go out and the provinces do as they please.
Precarious: half the great houses are waiting to see which way it falls.
Shaken: it can still act, but every action costs more than it should.
Working badly: the machinery grinds, yet the grain still gets counted.
Holding: it has problems and survives them.
Firm: its right to rule is rarely questioned aloud.
Strong, with a legitimacy that has survived two bad harvests.
Rock-solid: it has endured worse and been thanked for it.
Steady at the center, brittle at the edges.
Untested: nothing has threatened it, and nothing has tested it.
Confident, and overextended in three directions at once.
government_strength: Clerks who can count a province's grain before the harvest ends.
A legion that has never once been ordered against the ruler.
A name that still quiets a room when it is spoken.
Ownership of the salt pans and the good iron.
A promise of better times that the people still believe.
Envoys who can turn a war into a marriage in a single season.
A spymaster who reads the letters of three courts.
A bound spirit that answers questions the ruler has not thought to ask.
A temple that preaches the crown's cause in every village.
A bloodline whose children are born with the sight.
A river fleet that can starve a city without a siege.
A network of informers in every market town.
A granary that has never quite been emptied.
A fortress that has never been taken.
Coin in the vault while every rival is borrowing.
A marriage web that makes war within the realm a family matter.
A standing alliance with the hill clans, paid in tribute and respect.
A relic whose presence is said to decide battles.
